_comment: The page's opening URL, trick gallery (a card with hosts shows how Hrefine displays them, as the tours print it, with no recorded parsers), and table of more disagreements (corpus: groups of inputs, each with a short HTML note, and compare: "path" for path tricks, else hosts are compared). site/record/record.py records other parsers' answers for these inputs into site/recorded.json; site/build.py renders them. The explanations are HTML.

cards.title: Short addresses
cards.explain: Browsers read IPv4 addresses with missing parts, as the old inet_aton did, so 127.1 is 127.0.0.1. A parser that keeps the text lets it past a blocklist of 127.0.0.1, and the system's resolver usually connects to loopback anyway.

cards.title: Hex addresses
cards.explain: Parts in hex (or octal, with a leading 0) are numbers too. A check that looks for internal addresses as text misses them; Hrefine says the host is an IPv4 address, whatever it looks like.

cards.title: One big number
cards.explain: A whole address as one decimal number, 127 × 2²⁴ + 1. Python, Java, and Go keep it as text, and the browser reads loopback.

cards.title: Backslashes
cards.explain: Browsers treat \ as / in http and https URLs. Python and Go find no host here at all, so a host check has nothing to stop, and the browser goes to evil.example.

cards.title: Open redirects
cards.explain: A server checks that a next parameter is a path on its own site, and Python, Java's URL, C#, Go, and curl all say it is. The browser, resolving it against the page, goes to evil.example.

cards.title: Who's the host?
cards.explain: Everything before @ is a user name, so the host is evil.example. Parsers agree; the trap is people, and checks like startsWith("https://good.example").

cards.title: Fragments with @
cards.explain: Everything after # is the fragment, so the host is evil.example. Parsers agree; a check that takes the text after the last @ reads good.example.

cards.title: Tabs and newlines
cards.explain: Browsers drop tabs and newlines anywhere in a URL, so this host ends in .evil.example. Strict parsers refuse it, which is safe only if nothing downstream reads it the browser's way.

cards.title: javascript:, hidden
cards.explain: A filter looking for javascript: misses it, but browsers drop the tab and run the script. Check the parsed scheme, never the text.

cards.title: Look-alike letters
cards.explain: The first letter is Cyrillic а, so browsers send xn--pple-43d.com, which isn't apple.com. Some parsers keep the Unicode, so a check and a request can see different names. This is the long-known IDN homograph trick.

cards.title: Look-alike hosts
cards.explain: Every letter is Cyrillic, but each looks Latin, so browsers show the xn-- form instead. Hrefine's display form decides as Chrome does, from Unicode's data.

hosts.note: All Cyrillic, but every letter looks Latin: a whole-script look-alike of apple.com.
The same letters under .рф, a Cyrillic top-level domain, where readers expect Cyrillic.
One Cyrillic а among Latin letters: mixed scripts.
Russian for “example”, with Cyrillic letters that don't look Latin.

cards.why: Anyone can register names like these, so browsers check each label's letters against Unicode's data. Its scripts must go together: one script, or the mixes Chinese, Japanese, and Korean use. And a label whose every letter looks Latin keeps xn-- unless the top-level domain is in its own script. UrlDisplay.addressBar and domainToDisplay follow these rules. Show people that form, but decide, and hand on, with href, which is always ASCII.

cards.title: Dots that aren't dots
cards.explain: Browsers read the ideographic full stop 。 as a dot, so this is a name under evil.example. Parsers without IDNA see one odd label, and a check for names ending in .evil.example misses it.

cards.title: Protocol-relative
cards.explain: It starts with /, so it looks like a path on your own site, but // starts a host. Every parser agrees; the trap is checks like startsWith("/").

cards.title: Too many slashes
cards.explain: Browsers and curl skip extra slashes and find evil.example. Python, Java, and Go see no host, and C# refuses it.

items.note: Browsers end the host at \; Python keeps it in the host.
Two backslashes start a host, as // does.
The tab goes, leaving //evil.example: an open redirect past a check for //.
One slash and one backslash still start the host.
Browsers trim leading control characters, so this runs as javascript:.
An escaped tab in a host is an error to browsers; Python and Java keep it as text.
A NUL in the host: curl stops reading at it, and finds good.example.
The tab goes, so ..\t is .., and the path is /b.
The last @ ends the user info, so the host is evil.example.
An escaped @ decodes into the host, where it's forbidden.
From Orange Tsai's talk: three hosts to pick from. Browsers pick 2.2.2.2.
Looks like a host and port, but it's a user and password. Parsers agree; people don't.
A leading 0 means octal: 0177 is 127.
The whole address as one hex number.
Padded with zeros, so octal, and still loopback.
0.0.0.0, which reaches the local machine on many systems.
Browsers drop an address's trailing dot; others keep it, past a blocklist.
An escaped 127.1. curl decodes it but keeps the short form.
One past the largest address: browsers refuse it, and every other parser takes it as a name.
Five numbers, which browsers refuse, since it ends in a number but isn't an address.
Zone IDs aren't in the standard, so browsers refuse them; curl drops the zone.
A dot after the brackets: only C# accepts it.
Loopback, as an IPv4-mapped IPv6 address. Parsers agree; a blocklist of IPv4 text misses it.
Browsers decode escapes in a host: this is evil.example.
An escaped dot, decoded, splits the label.
An escaped slash decodes into the host, where it's forbidden.
Full-width letters map to ASCII, by IDNA.
So do circled letters.
An invisible soft hyphen, which IDNA drops.
Today's IDNA keeps ß (xn--fa-hia), where the older IDNA 2003 made it fass.example, another name.
A trailing dot: the same name to DNS, but not to an allowlist that compares text.
Three slashes, and browsers still find a host.
A backslash and a slash start a host too.
No slashes at all, and browsers still find a host.
Against an https page, a new scheme without slashes still names a host.
But with the page's own scheme, it's a path on the page's host.
One slash is enough for browsers.
Ports stop at 65535; Python, Java, and Go take it.
Browsers refuse a hex port; Python and Java's URI don't.
A space before the port: Python ignores it.
Browsers read %2e%2e as .., so the path is /admin, past a check for /public/.
Backslashes are slashes in browsers, so this is /admin too.
Dot segments resolve, and can't climb above the root.
An escaped slash isn't a slash to browsers, but C# decodes the dots.
Spaces are escaped as %20, not refused.
Non-ASCII is escaped as UTF-8.
A % without hex digits stays as it is; C# escapes it again.
Browsers leave | as it is, which RFC 3986 doesn't allow: Java's URI refuses it, even in href, and C# escapes it.
